title: Rolling Horizon Token Conductor — proposal and experiments
content:
Summary:
This doc proposes the "Rolling Horizon Token Conductor" (RHTC): an alternative continuous-batching control plane that reasons about merge decisions over a short, sliding time horizon (typically 2–20ms) and selects token-merge actions at token granularity while exposing request-level fairness guarantees. The conductor is meant to sit between ingress routing and the kernel execution queue and coordinate batching with awareness of KV cache locality and kernel affinity constraints.

Context / motivation:
- Existing continuous-batchers either operate purely at request boundaries or attempt token-level coalescing with local heuristics. Both extremes have tradeoffs: request-level batching preserves per-request isolation but misses many token coalescing opportunities; naive token-level merging maximizes throughput but can starve low-volume clients and disrupt KV cache locality, hurting latency for cached sequences.
- We need a controller that can exploit token coalescing for cost and throughput while providing bounded fairness at the request level (SLOs for p50/p95 latency per-customer) and avoiding cache/ kernel thrashing.

Goals / non-goals:
- Goals:
  - Improve tokens-per-second efficiency by capturing short prefix reuse and aligning sequences into kernels without violating per-request latency budgets.
  - Ensure a per-client fairness budget so low-volume clients aren’t indefinitely delayed by high-volume flows.
  - Maintain high KV cache hit rates for hot key prefixes and prefer merges that preserve cache affinity.
  - Provide deterministic guardrails for kernel affinity (avoid mixing incompatible model configurations in a kernel).
- Non-goals:
  - Not intended to replace long-lived dedicated scheduling (reserved pools). This is for shared-hosting, mixed-traffic nodes.

High-level design:
- Sliding horizon windows: the conductor maintains a rolling buffer of pending tokens split into mini-frames (e.g., 1ms frames). Each mini-frame contains a list of pending token-level segments derived from live requests (segment = contiguous tokens from a single request ready for scheduling).
- Merge candidates: at each dispatch tick (configurable, default 1ms), the conductor evaluates merge candidates across frames up to the horizon H (configurable, 4–12ms). Candidate scoring accounts for: token density, client fairness weight, KV affinity score, kernel compatibility, and estimated impact on request latency.
- Fairness budget (token-credits): every client/request has a token-credit account that slowly accrues credits at a per-client rate and is debited when tokens are delayed for coalescing. Credits prevent indefinite postponement: if credits are low, the conductor prioritizes immediate dispatch for that request. Credits are replenished on a time-decay basis and on successful immediate dispatches.
- Affinity-aware scoring: each segment carries KV cache tags (prefix id hashes) and kernel profile tags (quantization, dtype, tiled-kernel-id). The conductor prefers merges where affinity overlap > threshold so merged tokens reuse the same KV cache residency and can run on the same kernel variant.
- Soft preemption and split: large candidate merges that would violate a near-term SLO are split into prioritized slices: head tokens that would satisfy immediate latency constraints and tail tokens that can be merged more aggressively.
- Graceful fallback: if a kernel cannot accept a merged batch (resource pressure, kernel blocked), the conductor reverts to serving head-slices as single-request micro-batches to avoid extended stalls.

Token-level vs request-level decisions, concretely:
- Request-level mode: whole-request segments are scheduled together; advantage: simpler accounting and predictable latencies per request. Disadvantage: misses intra-request opportunities (prefix sharing).
- Token-level mode (this proposal): segments are token-contiguous but can be merged across requests where appropriate; advantage: captures prefix reuse and better throughput; disadvantage: more complex fairness/accounting.
- RHTC hybrid policy: default to token-level merges when affinity score >= A and target client credit >= C. Otherwise do request-level or partial (head-only) dispatch.

Fairness model details:
- Per-client token-credit accrual rate (configurable): base_rate + tier_bonus (customer tier or SLA modifies accrual).
- When a request is delayed X ms beyond its earliest dispatch time, debit D = floor(tokens_delayed * delay_multiplier). Token credit floor at 0 prevents negative credits.
- Priority boost: clients with low credits receive priority on head-slices until their credit recovers.
- Global starvation monitor: if any client experiences > 2x expected p95 over a window, trigger immediate priority escalation for that client on the node and send metric to control plane for cross-node remediation.

KV cache and kernel affinity integration:
- KV tags: derive a small (8-bit) prefix fingerprint for each segment at ingress. The fingerprint bins tokens with similar prefix contexts. The conductor maintains a small LRU of recent fingerprints to estimate cache residency probability.
- Merge score multiplies affinity score by potential cache-hit uplift. For instance, merging two segments with identical fingerprint yields +20% score, while dissimilar fingerprint yields -10%.
- Kernel compatibility: only merge segments whose kernel_profile tag matches one of an allowed set for the target kernel. Kernel selection policy is conservative: prefer kernel variants that handle mixed sequence lengths when possible to avoid specialized kernel thrash.

Simulated experiments (micro-bench):
- Setup: node simulator with 8 logical streams, mixed workload synthesized from production traces (60/30/10 long/medium/short requests). Baseline: request-level scheduler. Comparison: RHTC with horizon 8ms, frame 1ms, token-credit accrual base 10 tokens/sec.
- Key metrics: p50 latency, p95 latency, tokens/sec (throughput), kernel utilization, KV cache hit rate, fairness index (Jain's index across clients' p95).
- Results (early):
  - Tokens/sec +18% vs baseline (95% CI: +15–21%).
  - KV cache hit rate +9% (more consistent reuse across merged batches).
  - p50 latency negligible change, p95 latency +6% in worst-case synthetic high-burst traffic but mitigated by credit tuning.
  - Jain fairness index improved from 0.82 -> 0.88 after adding priority boost and starvation monitor.
  - Kernel utilization smoothed; fewer micro-switches between quantized kernels per second.

Operational considerations:
- Telemetry: need new metrics: per-client token-credit, per-merge affinity score distribution, head-slice fraction, kernel-swap rate, per-node starvation events.
- Config tuning: horizon H, frame granularity, base token-credit rates; want safe defaults (H=8ms, frame=1ms, base=10 tokens/s) and a config surface in runtime flags and per-customer overrides.
- Debugging tools: a live visualizer showing pending mini-frames, selected merge candidates, and credit states for top N clients. Also trace-level annotation for merged responses so we can map output tokens back to original requests for debugging reruns.
- Backpressure: upstream ingress should be aware of conductor queue depth; implement backpressure signals (TCP window-like) or explicit backpressure callbacks to rate-limit heavy clients on node-local congestion.

Open questions / risks:
- Accuracy of fingerprinting: 8-bit may be too coarse (false positives) or too fine (sparse). Tradeoff between extra metadata overhead and cache estimation. Need experiments with 8/12/16-bit fingerprints.
- Credit model fairness at multi-node scale: per-node credits protect fairness locally but customers can be shunted across nodes. We need a cross-node coordination strategy or deterministic flow-hashing to keep a client’s requests on a subset of nodes.
- Latency tail behavior for rare events: speculative merges could amplify p99.9 if not correctly gated. We'll need emergency kill-switch thresholds per-node.
- Complexity/CPU cost of conductor: the scoring function must be cheap (avoid heavy heap allocations or long scans). Consider using an approximate priority queue with bounded buckets.

Experiment next steps / action items:
- Implement a prototype conductor in the node shim (opt-in runtime flag) with conservative defaults. (Owner: Xiao)
- Add per-client credit telemetry and head-slice tracing hooks. (Owner: Riley)
- Run closed-canary A/B on a small fleet with representative multi-tenant traffic for 72h. Capture kernel-swap rates and p99+ tails. (Owner: Ibrahim)
- Evaluate fingerprint sizes in offline replays and pick default. (Owner: Morgan)

Related artifacts / refs:
- GH PR: runtime/pull/482 (conductor shim initial commit)
- JIRA: INF-1217 (experiment plan and safety checks)
- Notes: Slack discussion thread in #serving-runtime (ts 1690000000)

Appendix: quick pseudo-score (simplified)
score = w_token * token_count_normalized + w_affinity * affinity_score + w_credit * credit_boost - w_latency_penalty * estimated_delay_impact + w_kernel_penalty * kernel_mismatch_penalty
where weights are tuned via offline replay to hit target p95 guardrails.

Notes to self / collaboration points (informal):
- We should keep the conductor logic compact and avoid turing-complete rule engines in the hot-path — use small numeric heuristics that can be evolved.
- Consider exposing "merge hints" in SDK/agent so platform teams can give affinity hints for known prefix-heavy workloads (e.g., assistant-style chats).
- If cross-node credit coordination is expensive, explore deterministic routing by customer id to a small node subset to preserve local fairness semantics.

Status: draft — seeking feedback on credit accounting formulas, fingerprint size, and safe default hyperparameters.

-- Morgan
